findings.fix: Reorder the step divs in the DOM to match the visual order (Choose plan, Enter payment, Confirm), or remove the CSS order property and reorder visually.
findings.evidence: DOM order: Confirm your order (step 3), Enter payment details (step 2), Choose a plan (step 1). CSS order property reverses visual order to: Choose a plan (1), Enter payment details (2), Confirm your order (3).
findings.violation: The DOM order does not match the visual order created by CSS order property, so a screen-reader user reading linearized content encounters steps in reverse sequence, reversing the actual decision flow.

findings.fix: Add an asterisk or the word required to the label text, or add aria-required="true" to the input field itself.
findings.evidence: Label text rendered in red (#cc0000) via inline style attribute, with no asterisk, no required attribute, no aria-required, no other non-color signal.
findings.violation: The required state is marked only by color (red text), with no accompanying text label, asterisk, or other visual signal, so a color-blind reader cannot tell this field is required until submitting the form.

findings.fix: Replace error text with a specific message like 'Invalid promo code format' or 'Promo code not found'.
findings.evidence: Error message reads 'Error.' with no description of the problem. Associated input has aria-invalid="true" (identifying the field) but error text alone is generic.
findings.violation: The error message is generic and fails to describe what is wrong with the promo code input, only stating that an error exists.

findings.fix: Add role="button" to the div, set aria-label="Delete" (or descriptive text), and add aria-pressed or another state attribute if it toggles.
findings.violation: A custom control built from a div carries no role, no accessible name, and no state exposed programmatically, so assistive technology cannot determine what this component is or what activating it does.
